title: Sunni and Shia today
hookLine: Sunni and Shia Muslims today, two families of one faith, praying side by side
tomorrow: Block C close: the wound and the healing

lines: HANDS FOLDED, HANDS AT THE SIDES.
THE SAME MOMENT, THE SAME WAY.
cards: A row of people in prayer, shoulder to shoulder. The man on the left has his hands folded over his chest. The man on the right lets his arms hang at his sides.

When they go down into prostration, one sets his forehead on a small disc of baked clay he carried in his pocket. The other puts his forehead straight on the carpet. Then they rise at the same moment, facing the same way.
From the back of the room you might guess one is Sunni and one is Shia. You might be wrong. Today: Sunni and Shia today.

teach.h: THE SAME KAABA, THE SAME ARAFAT.
teach.b: Sunni and Shia Muslims share cities, streets, and sometimes houses. At the pilgrimage in Mecca, pilgrims from both walk around the same Kaaba, stand on the same plain of Arafat, and throw stones at the same pillars.
No one checks which telling of the succession you hold. In some cities there are mosques where both pray in the same rows.
In some families, a Sunni mother and a Shia father, or the reverse, raise children who know both ways of standing. The differences you can see are small and real.

Shia practice is to pray with arms at the sides and to prostrate on natural earth, such as a clay tablet called a turbah, since Shia jurists teach that the forehead should rest on earth or what grows from it.
Folded hands are the Sunni posture people tend to picture. But in the Maliki school of Sunni law, praying with arms at the sides is an accepted practice too.
So the hands alone sort nobody.

And scholars of the schools, Sunni and Shia, have put their names to a statement issued in Amman, recognizing one another's schools as Muslim and saying their followers may not be declared outside the faith.
Statements don't end every quarrel. But they say where the scholars chose to stand.

how: Sunni and Shia Muslims perform the same pilgrimage rites in Mecca, and in some cities pray in the same mosques; Shia worshipers prostrate on earth, such as a clay tablet, and pray with arms at their sides, as some Maliki Sunnis also do.

o: a prayer rug woven with a picture of the Kaaba
a small cap worn by men during the prayer
a clay tablet for the forehead in prostration

games.q: Sunni and Shia today — tap the pairs.
p: a clay tablet for the forehead
Sunni, arms at the sides too
a plain where pilgrims from both stand
a statement recognizing each other's schools

s: you can always tell a Sunni from a Shia by their hands in prayer
in the Maliki school of Sunni law, arms at the sides is accepted too.
Sunni and Shia pilgrims walk around the same Kaaba
both perform the pilgrimage at the same places in Mecca.
the clay tablet is placed under the forehead in prostration
Shia jurists teach the forehead should rest on earth or what grows from it.

games.q: you arrive at a mosque in a new city. the row has gaps. the man beside one gap prays with his arms at his sides. what do you do?
o: find a different gap further down.
stand next to him and fill the row.
games.why: rows in prayer are filled shoulder to shoulder; Sunni and Shia Muslims can and do stand in the same row.

practice: Picture a line of people in prayer, each standing a little differently, all facing one way, and put yourself in the line.
Then bring to mind someone you live or work beside who sees the world differently from you, and stand with them there, in your mind, for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Turbah, earth or soil: the clay tablet some Shia worshipers rest their foreheads on in prostration, one of the small, visible differences between Sunni and Shia Muslims who pray in the same rows. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: earth or soil; the clay tablet Shia worshipers place under the forehead in prostration.

carryVoice: Your line: side by side. Different hands, the same row, the same moment. Day nine hundred one.

sources.ref: The Amman Message and its scholars' statement (recognition of the Sunni and Shia schools of law; against declaring other Muslims apostates)
Maliki fiqh on sadl (arms at the sides in prayer), e.g. the Mudawwana of Sahnun
Twelver Shia fiqh on prostration on earth or what grows from it (turbah)
